content_list.content_text: The films of this period bring certain images to mind: James Cagney (1899-1986) pushing a grapefruit into Mae Clarke's (1910-1992) face in The Public Enemy (1931), Paul Muni (1895-1967) brandishing his machine gun in Scarface (1932) and Edward G. Robinson (1893-1973) and his stocky, fedora-wearing mob boss in Little Caesar (1931). These three productions form what critics call the paradigm of the classic gangster film.

information.contentText: Real machine-gun bullets were used during the machine-gun attack on Tom Powers and his best friend Matt Doyle. A firearms expert stood on a raised platform 15 to 6 meters from the target and, when James Cagney's face disappeared behind the corner of the wall, he opened fire and created that tight cluster of machine-gun bullets.

content_list.content_text: Although the 1930s were an especially fertile period for gangster films, the one considered the first example of the genre was made almost 20 years earlier: D. W. Griffith's (1875-1948) The Musketeers of Pig Alley (1912), a 16-minute silent short film based on the real-life murder of gambler Herman Rosenthal. Another key gangster film of the late 1920s was Josef von Sternberg's (1894-1969) Underworld (1927), written by former Chicago reporter Ben Hecht. "I had an idea. The trick was to skip the heroes and heroines and write a movie containing only villains and bawds," Hecht explained in a revealing passage of his autobiography. "As a newspaperman, I had learned that the good folk - the public - loved criminals, and were crazy to read about their love troubles and their sadism."

In the previous decade, gangster films were spurred on by an unlikely group - the U.S. Congress - when, in the fall of 1919, the Volstead Act, which banned the sale of alcohol, was passed. Prohibition fostered the growth of criminal gangs, which seized the opportunity to offer Americans illegal access to liquor.

This was the era of crime bosses, bootleggers and speakeasies. It also represented a brave new world of opportunity for Hollywood. Some studios specialized in gangster films. Warner Bros., which liked to boast of making films "ripped from the headlines," was one of the most prominent. Little Caesar, directed by Mervyn LeRoy (1900-1987) and starring Edward G. Robinson as a short, psychotic hoodlum; William Wellman's (1896-1975) The Public Enemy (1931), with Cagney as an enterprising gangster (both from Warner); and Scarface (1932), from United Artists, directed by Howard Hawks (1896-1977), were released one after another and spawned a series of imitations.

content_list.title: Prohibition in the US
content_list.description:
In short, Prohibition, also known as the Prohibition era (Prohibition in the United States), refers to the period from 1920 to 1933 during which the manufacture, transportation and sale of alcoholic beverages for consumption were banned nationwide, as stipulated by the 18th Amendment to the United States Constitution.

By the late 1920s, alcohol use had become a symbolic arena for a more general conflict within the American middle class. Prohibition, originally adopted with strong popular support, ended up making drinking a perfect symbol of generational revolt, "the symbol of a sacred cause," as Liebling recalled. Although Prohibition had reduced overall consumption by two-thirds at its most effective, and still by one-third around 1930, middle-class consumption levels as a whole were little affected.

In the years before Prohibition, the movies had been seen as a great support for the cause of "temperance," both by the "wets" and - more mistakenly - by the "drys." First of all, they were the most attractive substitutes ever devised for saloons and bars. At the time, Chicago police officials estimated that they had cut the saloon trade in half in a North Side district. Temperance melodramas, a specific genre that reached great popularity until the end of the 1920s, aimed to combat alcohol consumption and support Prohibition. 'Dry propaganda' films such as Prohibition (1915), directed by Hal Reid, Distilled Spirits (1915), directed by Milton J. Fahrney, and The Curse of Drink (1922), directed by Harry O. Hoyt, are examples of this genre.

But this changed in the late 1920s. Ten Nights in a Barroom was released in two versions at the time, in 1926 and 1930, and the 1930 version already presented the view of a population opposed to the law. In one scene, the town doctor looks back on the old days and tells his cronies, who are turning against Prohibition, about the evils of the old-time saloon.

The effect of the law was the complete opposite of what was expected. Instead of ending alcohol consumption, social problems and other ills, the law led to the discrediting of the authorities, increased corruption, crime surges in several states and the enrichment of the mafias that controlled the bootlegging of alcoholic beverages. The meeting places for people who wanted to drink were clandestine underground bars, designed not to draw attention. Arguing that legalizing alcohol would create more jobs, boost the economy and increase tax revenue, opponents of then-U.S. president Franklin Roosevelt convinced him to ask the United States Congress to legalize beer. As a result, in 1933 the Prohibition constitutional amendment was repealed.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the articles "The movies and the wettening of America: the media as amplifiers of cultural change" by Robin Room, and Prohibition on wikipedia.com.

content_list.content_text: Scarface, written by Hecht, was based on the story of crime boss Al Capone (played with flamboyant affectation by Muni). "I'd like to do the Capone family as if they were the Borgias set down in Chicago," Hawks told Hecht. Unlike earlier films in the genre, Scarface did not slip past the censors. "The American public and the conscientious State Boards of Censorship find gangsters and hoodlums repugnant. Gangsterism must not be mentioned in the cinema," the Hays Office informed Hawks on the eve of production. Hawks shot the film anyway, but afterward he and producer Howard Hughes faced a Herculean battle to secure its release.

The concessions demanded of Hawks and Hughes before Scarface could reach theaters proved a discouraging example for future producers of gangster films. The censors wanted the film retitled "The Shame of a Nation" and wanted the antihero to reveal himself as a coward in the final scenes and be hanged. Yet the censors could hardly accuse Hollywood of inventing its gangster stories at a time when such stories were constantly on the front pages of the newspapers. The line between real-life criminals and their celluloid counterparts often seemed thin. John Dillinger, one of the most famous gangsters of the period, was shot dead in 1934 as he left a Chicago movie theater, where he had gone to see a gangster picture starring Clark Gable (1901-1960), Manhattan Melodrama (1934).

information.contentText: At the time of its release, American film censors felt that Scarface made the criminal life look far too easy and suggested that Tony could get away with his crimes. As a result, a second ending was shot, showing Tony Camonte being arrested, tried, and sentenced to death in court. The scene of the death of Tony's sister, in which he reveals that his feelings for her are more than brotherly, was also re-edited. Since none of these changes satisfied the censors of the day, Howard Hawks decided to drop all of them and release the film without the censors' approval.

content_list.content_text: There is an essential tension in the gangster film that defines it as a genre. This tension is obvious from the very first of them, but it is especially prevalent in the 1930s. On the one hand, its heroes are glamorous, charismatic figures with whom audiences easily identify. But, on the other, they invariably turn out to be cruel, hateful killers who leave a trail of physical and emotional destruction wherever they go.

That is why they must be punished - and why Cagney's gangster in Angels with Dirty Faces (1938) goes so cowardly to the electric chair. Or at least he seems to. The film ends ambiguously: the viewer will never know whether Cagney is pretending to be afraid out of respect for his childhood friend Jerry Connolly (Pat O'Brien) - Connolly, now a priest, had asked him to die whimpering so that the kids he is trying to keep on the right side of the law won't idolize him - or whether he is truly terrified.

Gangster antiheroes hold a special fascination for those who wish to criticize the status quo. This was made clear in Robert Warshow's influential essay "The Gangster as Tragic Hero" (1948), written just after the genre's golden age in the 1930s and early 1940s. He argued that gangster films were "an expression of that part of the American psyche which (...) rejects Americanism".

information.contentTitle: The famous electric chair scene from Angels with Dirty Faces (1938)
information.contentText: Because of the controversy surrounding gangster films, this one was banned in Denmark, China, Poland, Finland and parts of Canada and Switzerland.

content_list.content_text: The United States as a political and social organization may have been committed to "a cheerful view of life," but Warshow believed that, deep down, this view was subverted by these films. He wrote about Hollywood's gangsters as if they were Shakespearean characters - heroes with fatal flaws. If gangster films created a new kind of Hollywood protagonist - the tough, urban, working-class hero - they also made America's obsession with violence abundantly clear.

Guns had been part of American films since Edwin S. Porter's (1870-1941) The Great Train Robbery (1903), but the boom of the early 1930s came just as Hollywood was making the transition to talkies - and only sound films could do justice to the "rat-a-tat-tat" of machine-gun fire from both FBI agents and gangsters. The gangsters - and especially those played by Cagney - used dialogue in an equally reckless and aggressive way. The best films of the genre also had the same vulgarity and realistic characterization found in the slangy short stories written by Damon Runyon (1880-1946) and Ring Lardner (1885-1933) during the period.

quote.quote: You want me, you're going to have to come and get me!
quote.author: Caesar Enrico Bandello - Little Caesar

content_list.content_text: Worried about the growing fame of criminals such as John Dillinger, the Hays Office censors banned gangster films in 1935. Hollywood's response was to move the bandit, or at least the actor who played him, to the side of the law. 'G' Men (1935) starred Cagney, one of the archetypal screen gangsters, now turned government agent as a lawyer working for the FBI.

In Hollywood, the brooding self-awareness of film noir only began to replace the genre in the 1940s. In this respect, tracing Humphrey Bogart's career is quite instructive. In The Petrified Forest (1936), he was Duke Mantee, a world-famous killer. In Dead End (1937), Angels with Dirty Faces (1938) and The Roaring Twenties (1939) he was still on the side of the bad guys.

information.contentTitle: James Cagney Meets The Dead End Kids
information.contentText: The Dead End Kids, a group of young New York actors, first appeared in Sidney Kingsley's play Dead End on Broadway in 1935. In 1937, producer Samuel Goldwyn brought them all to Hollywood and turned the play into a film. They proved so popular that they went on making films under various names, including Little Tough Guys (1938), East Side Kids (1940) and The Bowery Boys, until 1958.

content_list.content_text: However, his screen persona gradually changed. He began playing private detectives instead of criminals. As he metamorphosed, so did the genre. Productions such as Scarface and Little Caesar gave way to films in which detectives, not gangsters, were the heroes. Still, the bandits of Hollywood films of the 1920s and 1930s were also businessmen of a sort. Prohibition offered them a market gap that they exploited with the power of the gun. The Depression created an intimidating economic environment in which the criminal lifestyle seemed attractive.

By the 1950s, Prohibition was no longer in effect and the United States was going through a more prosperous time. Gangsters became the scum of society. The level of sadistic violence began to rise: in The Big Heat (1953), Lee Marvin throws a cup of scalding coffee in Gloria Grahame's face. In 1973, in The Long Goodbye (1973), Mark Rydell smashes a bottle into his girlfriend's face - not because she did anything wrong, but just to warn Philip Marlowe, played by Elliott Gould.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Geoffrey Macnab, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

movies.title: Scarface
movies.overview: A murderous thug shoots his way to the top of the mobs while trying to protect his sister from the criminal life.

movies.title: Little Caesar
movies.overview: A small-time hood shoots his way to the top, but how long can he stay there?

movies.title: The Public Enemy
movies.overview: Two young Chicago hoodlums, Tom Powers and Matt Doyle, rise up from their poverty-stricken slum life to become petty thieves, bootleggers and cold-blooded killers. But with street notoriety and newfound wealth, the duo feels the heat from the cops and rival gangsters both. Despite his ruthless criminal reputation, Tom tries to remain connected to his family, however, gang warfare and the need for revenge eventually pull him away.

movies.title: 'G' Men
movies.overview: James “Brick” Davis, a struggling attorney, owes his education to a mobster, but always has refused to get involved with the underworld. When a friend of his is gunned down by a notorious criminal, Brick decides to abandon the exercise of the law and join the Department of Justice to capture the murderer.

movies.title: Underworld
movies.overview: Boisterous gangster kingpin Bull Weed rehabilitates his former lawyer from his alcoholic haze, but complications arise when he falls for Weed's girlfriend.

movies.title: Angels with Dirty Faces
movies.overview: In New York, the boys Rocky Sullivan and Jerry Connelly are best friends and small time thieves. After a robbery, Rocky is arrested and sent to a reformatory school, where he begins his criminal career. Jerry escapes and later becomes a priest. After three years in prison, Rocky is released and demands the return of $100,000 deposited with his solicitor - prior to his jail term.

movies.title: Bullets or Ballots
movies.overview: After Police Captain Dan McLaren becomes police commissioner, former detective Johnny Blake publicly punches him, convincing rackets boss Al Kruger that Blake is sincere in his effort to join the mob. "Bugs" Fenner, meanwhile, is certain that Blake is a police agent.
